results.title: Class of finite groups (Kourovka 10.72)

results.summary: A class of finite groups is given by a membership predicate: a proposition $X(G)$ for every finite group $G$. It is not required to be closed under isomorphisms.

results.title: Formation of finite groups (Kourovka 10.72)
results.caption: Definition

results.title: Permutation groups isomorphic to the rationals have infinite displacement (Kourovka 20.98)
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: For every subgroup $G$ of the group of permutations of $\mathbb{N} = \{0, 1, 2, \dots\}$ that is isomorphic to the additive group $(\mathbb{Q}, +)$, there is an element $g \in G$ such that the set of displacements $\{a - g(a) : a \in \mathbb{N}\}$, computed in $\mathbb{Z}$, is infinite. results.summary: A word $(d_1, \ldots, d_n)$ of direction labels in $\{0, 1, 2\}$ is self-avoiding when its set of visited vertices has exactly $n + 1$ elements, that is, when its $n + 1$ vertices, the $i$-th vertices for $0 \le i \le n$, are pairwise distinct.

results.title: Number of self-avoiding walks on the honeycomb lattice
results.caption: Definition
results.summary: For a natural number $n$, this is the number of self-avoiding walks with $n$ steps on the honeycomb lattice starting at the origin.

results.title: Three-step self-avoiding walks on the honeycomb lattice
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: There are exactly $12$ self-avoiding walks with $3$ steps on the honeycomb lattice starting at a fixed vertex.

results.title: Six-step self-avoiding walks on the honeycomb lattice
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: There are exactly $90$ self-avoiding walks with $6$ steps on the honeycomb lattice starting at a fixed vertex.

results.title: The connective constant of the honeycomb lattice
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: Let $c_n$ be the number of $n$-step self-avoiding walks on the honeycomb lattice starting at the origin. Then $c_n^{1/n} \to \sqrt{2 + \sqrt{2}}$ as $n \to \infty$.

results.title: Rice–Shapiro, upward closure
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: In a class with a recognizable index set, every partial recursive extension of a partial recursive member is a member.

results.title: Rice–Shapiro, finite approximation
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: Every partial recursive member of a class with a recognizable index set has a partial recursive finite subfunction in the class.

results.title: Finite function of a list of pairs
results.caption: Definition
results.summary: For a finite list $\theta$ of pairs of natural numbers, the finite function of $\theta$ is the partial function $\mathbb{N} \rightharpoonup \mathbb{N}$ whose value at $x$ is the second component of the first pair in $\theta$ with first component $x$, and which is undefined at $x$ when $\theta$ has no pair with first component $x$.

results.title: Graphs of finite functions
results.caption: Definition
results.summary: A finite list $\theta$ of pairs of natural numbers is a graph when, for every pair $(x, y)$ in $\theta$, the finite function of $\theta$ takes the value $y$ at $x$; that is, the first pair in $\theta$ with first component $x$ is $(x, y)$.

results.title: Being a graph is recursively enumerable
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: The set of finite lists of pairs of natural numbers that are graphs is recursively enumerable.

results.title: Finite-domain partial functions are finite functions
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: For every partial function $g : \mathbb{N} \rightharpoonup \mathbb{N}$ with finite domain there is a finite list $\theta$ of pairs of natural numbers such that the finite function of $\theta$ is $g$ and, for every pair $(x, y)$ in $\theta$, $g(x)$ is defined and equals $y$.

results.title: Treap trees
results.caption: Inductive
results.summary: For a type $\kappa$ of keys and a type $\nu$ of values, a treap tree is either empty or a node made of a left subtree, a key in $\kappa$, a value in $\nu$, a natural-number priority and a right subtree. Trees are finite, and no ordering of keys or priorities is imposed; the treap invariants are stated separately.

results.title: Treap predicate holding at every node
results.caption: Definition
results.summary: Let $p$ be a predicate on a key, a value and a natural-number priority. A tree satisfies $p$ at every node when $p(k, v, n)$ holds for the key $k$, value $v$ and priority $n$ of each of its nodes. By recursion, this holds for the empty tree, and holds for a node exactly when it holds for the left subtree, $p$ holds at the node's key, value and priority, and it holds for the right subtree.

results.title: Entry membership in a treap tree
results.caption: Definition
results.summary: A key $k$, value $v$ and priority $p$ form an entry of a treap tree when some node stores exactly $k$, $v$ and $p$: the empty tree has no entries, and $(k, v, p)$ is an entry of a node with left subtree $L$, root key $r$, root value $w$, root priority $q$ and right subtree $R$ exactly when it is an entry of $L$, or $k = r$, $v = w$ and $p = q$, or it is an entry of $R$.

results.title: Key membership in a treap tree
results.caption: Definition
results.summary: A key $k$ is a key of a treap tree when it is stored at some node: no key belongs to the empty tree, and $k$ belongs to a node with left subtree $L$, root key $r$ and right subtree $R$ exactly when $k$ belongs to $L$, or $k = r$, or $k$ belongs to $R$.

results.title: Treap inorder traversal onto a suffix
results.caption: Definition
results.summary: For a tree $t$ and a list $s$ of key-value pairs, the traversal of $t$ onto $s$ is defined by recursion: for the empty tree it is $s$, and for a node with left subtree $l$, key $k$, value $v$ and right subtree $r$ it is the traversal of $l$ onto the list obtained by putting $(k, v)$ in front of the traversal of $r$ onto $s$. The result is the key-value pairs of $t$ in inorder, priorities dropped, followed by $s$.

results.title: Treap inorder contents
results.caption: Definition
results.summary: The contents of a tree $t$ is the list of its key-value pairs in inorder (left subtree, then node, then right subtree), with priorities dropped. It is defined as the inorder traversal of $t$ onto the empty list, which takes linear time.

results.title: Treap inorder contents of a node
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: For trees $l$ and $r$, a key $k$, a value $v$ and a natural-number priority $n$, the inorder list of key-value pairs of the node with left subtree $l$, key $k$, value $v$, priority $n$ and right subtree $r$ is the inorder list of $l$, followed by $(k, v)$, followed by the inorder list of $r$.

results.title: Size of a treap tree
results.caption: Definition
results.summary: The size of a tree is its number of nodes, computed recursively: the empty tree has size $0$, and a node with left subtree $L$ and right subtree $R$ has size equal to the size of $L$ plus one plus the size of $R$.

results.title: Ordered treap tree
results.caption: Definition
results.summary: For a key type equipped with a relation $<$, a treap tree is ordered when it is empty, or when it is a node with key $k$ whose left and right subtrees are both ordered, every key $x$ in the left subtree satisfies $x < k$, and every key $y$ in the right subtree satisfies $k < y$.

results.title: Heap order of treap priorities
results.caption: Definition
results.summary: A tree is heap-ordered when the priority of every node is at most the priority of every node below it. Recursively, the empty tree is heap-ordered, and a node with priority $p$ is heap-ordered when its left and right subtrees are heap-ordered and every node in them has priority at least $p$.

results.title: Valid treap
results.caption: Definition
results.summary: A binary tree whose nodes each carry a key, a value and a natural-number priority, with keys compared by a relation $<$ (any `LT` instance; no order axioms are assumed), is a valid treap when it satisfies both of the following at every node: every key in the left subtree is less than the node's key and the node's key is less than every key in the right subtree (search-tree order with respect to $<$), and the node's…

results.title: Treap lookup
results.caption: Definition
results.summary: Looking up a key $k$ in a tree with keys in a linearly ordered type follows the binary search tree comparisons. The empty tree gives no value. At a node with key $r$ and value $v$, the lookup continues in the left subtree if $k < r$, continues in the right subtree if $r < k$, and otherwise returns $v$.

results.title: Lookup with cost
results.caption: Definition
results.summary: The costed lookup of a key $k$ in a tree with keys in a linearly ordered type returns a possibly absent value together with a natural number counting the visited nodes. On the empty tree it returns no value and cost $0$. At a node with key $r$ and value $v$, if $k < r$ it returns the result of the costed lookup of $k$ in the left subtree with cost increased by $1$; if $r < k$ it does the same with the right…

results.title: Root priority of a treap tree
results.caption: Definition
results.summary: The root priority of a treap tree is an optional natural number: it is absent for the empty tree, and for a node it is the priority stored at that node.

results.title: Treap merge
results.caption: Definition
results.summary: The merge of two treap trees is defined recursively. Merging the empty tree with a tree $T$, or $T$ with the empty tree, gives $T$. If both trees are nodes, with root priorities $p$ for the first and $q$ for the second, then when $p \le q$ the result keeps the root of the first tree and its left subtree, and its right subtree is the merge of the first tree's right subtree with the second tree; otherwise the result…

results.title: Result of a treap split
results.caption: Structure
results.summary:
For key type $\kappa$ and value type $
u$, a split result consists of a lower tree, an optional entry given by a value in $
u$ together with a natural-number priority, and an upper tree, where both trees are treap trees with keys in $\kappa$ and values in $
u$.

results.title: Treap split
results.caption: Definition
results.summary: Let the keys come from a linear order, and write $(L, k, v, q, R)$ for the node with left subtree $L$, key $k$, value $v$, priority $q$ and right subtree $R$. Splitting a tree at a pivot $p$ returns a split result, defined by recursion on the tree. The empty tree splits into two empty trees and no entry. For a node $(L, k, v, q, R)$: if $k < p$, split $R$ at $p$ into a lower tree $R_1$, an optional entry $e$ and an…

results.title: Treap insertion
results.caption: Definition
results.summary: For a key $k$ of a linearly ordered key type, a value $v$, a priority $p$ and a tree $t$, inserting $k$ with value $v$ and priority $p$ into $t$ splits $t$ at $k$, drops the entry the split finds at $k$ if any, merges the part below $k$ with the single node $(k, v, p)$, and then merges the result with the part above $k$; all merges are priority-guided.

results.title: Treap deletion
results.caption: Definition
results.summary: For a key $k$ of a linearly ordered key type and a tree $t$, deleting $k$ from $t$ splits $t$ at $k$ and returns the priority-guided merge of the part of the split below $k$ with the part above $k$; the entry the split finds at $k$, if any, is dropped.

results.title: Treap all-nodes predicate via node membership
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: Let $p$ be a predicate on a key, a value and a natural-number priority, and let $t$ be a tree. Then $p$ holds at every node of $t$ if and only if $p(k, v, n)$ holds for every key $k$, value $v$ and priority $n$ such that the entry $(k, v, n)$ occurs as a node of $t$.

results.title: Entry membership implies key membership in a treap
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: If a key $k$, value $v$ and priority $p$ form an entry of a treap tree $t$, that is, some node of $t$ stores exactly $k$, $v$ and $p$, then $k$ is a key of $t$.

results.title: Inorder contents list the treap's entries
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: For every tree $t$, key $k$ and value $v$, the pair $(k, v)$ occurs in the inorder key-value list of $t$ if and only if $t$ has a node with key $k$ and value $v$, for some priority.

results.title: Keys occurring in the inorder contents
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: For a key $k$ and a tree $t$, some pair $(k, v)$ occurs in the inorder list of key-value pairs of $t$ if and only if $k$ is the key of some node of $t$.

results.title: Treap all-nodes predicate on keys via key membership
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: Let $p$ be a predicate on keys and let $t$ be a tree. Then the key of every node of $t$ satisfies $p$ if and only if $p(k)$ holds for every key $k$ that occurs in $t$.

results.title: Inorder key list of a treap
results.caption: Definition
results.summary: The inorder key list of a tree $t$ is the list of first components of the inorder list of key-value pairs of $t$, that is, the keys of $t$ in inorder.

results.title: Inorder keys of a node
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: For trees $l$ and $r$, a key $k$, a value $v$ and a priority $p$, the inorder key list of the node with left subtree $l$, entry $(k, v, p)$ and right subtree $r$ is the inorder key list of $l$, followed by $k$, followed by the inorder key list of $r$.

results.title: The inorder key list lists exactly the keys of a treap
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: For every treap tree $t$ and key $k$, $k$ occurs in the inorder key list of $t$ if and only if $k$ is a key of $t$.

results.title: Inorder keys of an ordered treap are strictly increasing
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: Let the keys come from a linearly ordered type. If a treap tree $t$ is ordered, then its inorder key list is strictly increasing: each key in the list is smaller than every key after it.

results.title: Treap keys are distinct
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: For a linearly ordered key type, if a tree is ordered as a binary search tree (at every node, every key in the left subtree is smaller and every key in the right subtree is larger than the node's key), then its inorder key list has no duplicates.

results.title: Treap lookup finds exactly the stored entries
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: Let $t$ be a tree with keys in a linearly ordered type that is ordered as a binary search tree (every key in a left subtree is smaller and every key in a right subtree is larger than the node's key). For every key $k$ and value $v$, looking up $k$ in $t$ returns $v$ if and only if $t$ has a node with key $k$ and value $v$, for some priority.

results.title: Treap lookup agrees with the inorder contents
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: Let $t$ be a tree with keys in a linearly ordered type that is ordered as a binary search tree (every key in a left subtree is smaller and every key in a right subtree is larger than the node's key). For every key $k$ and value $v$, looking up $k$ in $t$ returns $v$ if and only if the pair $(k, v)$ occurs in the inorder key-value list of $t$.

results.title: Costed lookup returns the ordinary lookup result
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: For every tree $t$ with keys in a linearly ordered type and every key $k$, the value component of the costed lookup of $k$ in $t$ (ignoring the visit count) equals the result of looking up $k$ in $t$.

results.title: Lookup cost is at most the tree size
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: For every tree $t$ with keys in a linearly ordered type and every key $k$, the number of nodes visited by the costed lookup of $k$ in $t$ is at most the number of nodes of $t$.

results.title: The root of a heap-ordered tree has minimal priority
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: If a nonempty tree whose root has priority $p$ is heap-ordered, then every node of the tree, the root included, has priority at least $p$.

results.title: Keys of a merged treap
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: For all trees $l$ and $r$ and every key $k$, $k$ is the key of some node of the merge of $l$ and $r$ if and only if $k$ is the key of some node of $l$ or of some node of $r$.

results.title: Treap merge concatenates inorder contents
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: For trees $l$ and $r$, the inorder list of key-value pairs of the priority-guided merge of $l$ and $r$ is the inorder list of $l$ followed by the inorder list of $r$.

results.title: Separated treap trees
results.caption: Definition
results.summary: For keys equipped with a binary relation $<$, two trees $L$ and $R$ are separated when $a < b$ for every key $a$ occurring at a node of $L$ and every key $b$ occurring at a node of $R$.

results.title: Treap merge preserves search-tree order
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: Let the keys come from a linearly ordered type. If treap trees $L$ and $R$ are both ordered and every key of $L$ is smaller than every key of $R$, then the merge of $L$ and $R$ is ordered.

results.title: Merging preserves heap order
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: If two trees $l$ and $r$ are both heap-ordered in their priorities, then the priority-guided merge of $l$ and $r$ is heap-ordered.

results.title: Treap split preserves search-tree order
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: Let the keys come from a linearly ordered type and let $t$ be an ordered treap tree. For every pivot key $k$, the lower tree and the upper tree produced by splitting $t$ at $k$ are both ordered.

results.title: Treap split preserves heap order
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: Let the keys come from a linearly ordered type and let $t$ be a heap-ordered treap tree. For every pivot key $k$, the lower tree and the upper tree produced by splitting $t$ at $k$ are both heap-ordered.

results.title: Split bounds for an ordered treap
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: Let the keys come from a linear order and let $T$ be an ordered tree. For every pivot $p$, every key of the lower tree obtained by splitting $T$ at $p$ is strictly less than $p$, and every key of the upper tree is strictly greater than $p$.

results.title: Splitting a treap preserves validity
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: Let the keys come from a linear order. If a tree is a valid treap, then for every pivot $p$, both the lower tree and the upper tree obtained by splitting it at $p$ are valid treaps.

results.title: Merging separated treaps preserves validity
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: Let the keys come from a linear order. If $L$ and $R$ are valid treaps and every key of $L$ is strictly less than every key of $R$, then the merge of $L$ and $R$ is a valid treap.

results.title: Inserting into a treap preserves validity
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: Let the keys come from a linear order. If a tree is a valid treap, that is, its keys are in strict binary-search-tree order and its priorities are in min-heap order, then for every key $k$, value $v$ and natural-number priority $q$, the tree obtained by inserting $k$ with value $v$ and priority $q$ is again a valid treap.

results.title: Erasing from a treap preserves validity
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: Let the keys come from a linear order. If a tree is a valid treap, that is, its keys are in strict binary-search-tree order and its priorities are in min-heap order, then for every key $k$ the tree obtained by erasing $k$ from it is again a valid treap.

results.title: Treap inorder contents split at a pivot
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: Let the keys come from a linearly ordered type, let $t$ be a tree and $k$ a pivot key, and let splitting $t$ at $k$ produce a lower tree $L$, an optional value-priority pair found at $k$, and an upper tree $G$. Then the inorder list of key-value pairs of $t$ is the inorder list of $L$, followed by $(k, v)$ if the split found a pair with value $v$ (and by nothing if it found none), followed by the inorder list of $G$.

results.title: Treap inorder contents after insertion
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: Let the keys come from a linearly ordered type, let $t$ be a tree, $k$ a key, $v$ a value and $n$ a natural-number priority, and let $L$ and $G$ be the lower and upper trees produced by splitting $t$ at $k$. Then the inorder list of key-value pairs of the tree obtained by inserting $k$ with value $v$ and priority $n$ into $t$ is the inorder list of $L$, followed by $(k, v)$, followed by the inorder list of $G$.

results.title: Treap inorder contents after erasure
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: Let the keys come from a linearly ordered type, let $t$ be a tree and $k$ a key, and let $L$ and $G$ be the lower and upper trees produced by splitting $t$ at $k$. Then the inorder list of key-value pairs of the tree obtained by erasing $k$ from $t$ is the inorder list of $L$ followed by the inorder list of $G$.

results.title: Treap lookup after insertion
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: Let $t$ be a valid treap with keys in a linearly ordered type, that is, $t$ is ordered as a binary search tree by key and as a min-heap by priority. For every key $k$, value $v$ and priority $p \in \mathbb{N}$, looking up $k$ in the tree obtained by inserting $k$ with value $v$ and priority $p$ into $t$ returns $v$.

results.title: Erased keys are not found
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: Let $t$ be a valid treap with keys in a linearly ordered type, that is, $t$ is ordered as a binary search tree by key and as a min-heap by priority. For every key $k$, looking up $k$ in the tree obtained by erasing $k$ from $t$ returns no value.

results.title: Stack push
results.caption: Definition
results.summary: Stacks over a type $\alpha$ are lists of elements of $\alpha$, with the first element as the top. Pushing $v \in \alpha$ onto a stack $s$ returns the stack with top $v$ followed by the elements of $s$, at cost $1$ (one successful push event).

results.title: Stack pop
results.caption: Definition
results.summary: Stacks over a type $\alpha$ are lists of elements of $\alpha$, with the first element as the top. Popping the empty stack returns underflow (no value) at cost $0$. Popping a stack with top $v$ and remaining stack $t$ returns the pair $(v, t)$ at cost $1$ (one successful pop event).

results.title: Stack top
results.caption: Definition
results.summary: Stacks over a type $\alpha$ are lists of elements of $\alpha$, with the first element as the top. Reading the top of the empty stack returns underflow (no value) at cost $0$. Reading the top of a stack with top $v$ returns $v$ at cost $1$ (one successful top event); the stack itself is not returned or changed.

results.title: Result and cost of stack pop
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: Let $s$ be a stack over a type $\alpha$ (a list of elements of $\alpha$ whose first element is the top). If $s$ is empty, popping $s$ returns underflow (no value) at cost $0$. If $s$ has top $h$ and remaining stack $t$, popping $s$ returns the pair $(h, t)$ at cost $1$.

results.title: Result and cost of reading the stack top
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: Let $s$ be a stack over a type $\alpha$ (a list of elements of $\alpha$ whose first element is the top). If $s$ is empty, reading the top of $s$ returns underflow (no value) at cost $0$. If $s$ has top $h$, reading the top of $s$ returns $h$ at cost $1$.

results.title: MULTIPOP
results.caption: Definition
results.summary: For a stack $S$, stored as a list with its top first, and a natural number $k$, MULTIPOP of $S$ with count $k$ repeatedly removes the top element while the stack is nonempty and fewer than $k$ elements have been removed, and returns the remaining stack. Each removed element costs one unit, and nothing else is charged.

results.title: Result of MULTIPOP
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: For every stack $S$, stored as a list with its top first, and every natural number $k$, the stack returned by MULTIPOP of $S$ with count $k$ is $S$ with its top $k$ elements removed, or the empty stack if $S$ has fewer than $k$ elements.

results.title: Cost of MULTIPOP
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: For every stack $S$ and every natural number $k$, the cost of MULTIPOP of $S$ with count $k$ is $\min(|S|, k)$, where $|S|$ is the number of elements of $S$.

results.title: MULTIPOP with an integer count
results.caption: Definition
results.summary: For a stack $S$ and an integer $k$, MULTIPOP with integer count $k$ is MULTIPOP of $S$ with the natural count $\max(k, 0)$, with the same result and cost. In particular, a count $k \le 0$ removes nothing.

results.title: MULTIPOP with a nonpositive count does nothing
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: For every stack $S$ and every integer $k \le 0$, MULTIPOP with integer count $k$ applied to $S$ returns $S$ at cost $0$.

results.title: Stack operations for the MULTIPOP aggregate analysis
results.caption: Inductive
results.summary: For a type $\alpha$ of stack entries, a stack operation is one of the following: $\mathrm{PUSH}(x)$ for an element $x \in \alpha$, $\mathrm{POP}$, or $\mathrm{MULTIPOP}(k)$ for an integer count $k$.

results.title: Running a sequence of stack operations

results.summary: Given a stack $S$ and a finite sequence of operations, each a PUSH of a value, a POP or a MULTIPOP with an integer count, the operations are applied to $S$ in order. results.title: Running a PUSH agrees with the standalone PUSH
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: For every stack $S$, every value $x$ and every finite sequence $\sigma$ of stack operations, running PUSH $x$ followed by $\sigma$ on $S$ has the same result and cost as first performing the standalone PUSH of $x$ on $S$ and then running $\sigma$ on the resulting stack, the two costs being added.

results.title: Running a POP agrees with the standalone POP
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: For every stack $S$ and every finite sequence $\sigma$ of stack operations, running POP followed by $\sigma$ on $S$ has the same result and cost as first performing the standalone POP on $S$ and then, if it reports underflow, stopping with an error at no further cost, or, if it removes the top element and leaves the stack $S'$, running $\sigma$ on $S'$, the two costs being added.

results.title: Cost balance for stack operation sequences
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: For every stack $S$ and every finite sequence $\sigma$ of stack operations, if running $\sigma$ on $S$ succeeds with final stack $F$, then the cost of the run plus the number of elements of $F$ equals the number of elements of $S$ plus twice the number of PUSH operations in $\sigma$.

results.title: Aggregate cost of stack operation sequences
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: For every stack $S$ and every sequence of $n$ stack operations (PUSH, POP and MULTIPOP), if running the sequence on $S$ succeeds, that is, no POP meets an empty stack, then its cost is at most $|S| + 2n$, where $|S|$ is the number of elements of $S$.

results.title: Mixed-model association chi-squared statistic
results.caption: Definition
results.summary: The mixed-model (generalized-least-squares score) statistic `χ²(V) = (xᵀ V⁻¹ y)² / (xᵀ V⁻¹ x)` of the marker `x` for the phenotype `y` under the phenotypic covariance `V`. For positive definite `V` and `x ≠ 0` the denominator is positive.

results.title: Sherman–Morrison applied to the candidate marker
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: For positive definite `V₀` and `c ≥ 0`, `(V₀ + c x xᵀ)⁻¹ x = (1 + c xᵀ V₀⁻¹ x)⁻¹ • V₀⁻¹ x`.

results.title: Proximal contamination
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: Including the candidate marker `x` in the covariance, `V = V₀ + c x xᵀ` with `V₀` positive definite and `c ≥ 0`, divides the mixed-model statistic by `1 + c xᵀ V₀⁻¹ x`, for every phenotype vector `y`: `χ²(V₀ + c x xᵀ) = χ²(V₀) / (1 + c xᵀ V₀⁻¹ x)`.

results.title: Including the marker in the covariance never increases the statistic
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: Including the candidate marker in the covariance never increases the mixed-model statistic: `χ²(V₀ + c x xᵀ) ≤ χ²(V₀)` for positive definite `V₀` and `c ≥ 0`.
